title: Analyze Audio from Zoom Calls with AssemblyAI and Node.js
summary: Learn how to analyze audio from Zoom calls using AssemblyAI and Node.js.
body_text:
Including AI in virtual meetings can significantly enhance efficiency and the user experience, a trend confirmed by a recent insights report which found that AI has firmly made its home in end-user products. For example, AI speech services can provide and analyze transcriptions to provide various insights from the meeting, such as an actionable item list or a detailed summary. In this tutorial, you'll learn how to get and parse audio from a Zoom call, transcribe the audio using AssemblyAI, and then process and analyze the transcribed audio using AssemblyAI's LLM Gateway and Speech Understanding models. Overview of Zoom audio transcription options Zoom offers three audio transcription options: built-in cloud transcription (limited accuracy), saved recording transcription via API, and real-time streaming transcription via RTMP. For production applications requiring high accuracy and advanced features, external Voice AI APIs like AssemblyAI provide superior results, a fact underscored in a survey of tech leaders where 58% cited quality and performance and 47% cited accuracy as top factors for choosing a vendor. This tutorial covers two developer-focused methods: transcribing saved recordings and real-time audio streaming. Transcribing saved recordings : The most straightforward approach. You'll learn to take a local or cloud recording from Zoom and transcribe it with a simple API call. Capturing and transcribing live audio : A more advanced method that involves streaming a live Zoom call via RTMP to a custom server, saving the audio, and then transcribing the saved file. This is useful for post-call analysis without relying on Zoom's cloud recordings. True real-time transcription : For applications requiring immediate, low-latency transcription (like live captioning), AssemblyAI's real-time streaming API is the recommended solution. This tutorial focuses on the RTMP capture method for post-call processing. We'll start with the simplest method—transcribing a saved recording. Set up your development environment Set up your development environment with these commands: mkdir assemblyai-zoom && cd assemblyai-zoom npm init -y npm install assemblyai dotenv fluent-ffmpeg node-media-server Because we'll be using modern ES Module syntax ( import / export ), open the generated package.json file and add the following line inside the main JSON object: "type": "module", Package dependencies: assemblyai : The AssemblyAI Node.js SDK, which simplifies interaction with the AssemblyAI API. dotenv : Dotenv is a Node.js package that loads environmental variables into process.env . You'll need this package to manage your environmental variables. fluent-ffmpeg : This is a Node.js library that abstracts the complex command line usage of FFmpeg into a simple-to-use package. You'll need this package to process your audio before sending it to AssemblyAI. node-media-server : Node Media Server is a Node.js implementation of several media servers, including RTMP. You'll need this package to create your custom streaming server where you receive an RTMP stream. Get your free AssemblyAI API key Create a free account to access your API key and start transcribing Zoom recordings with the Node.js SDK. Sign up free Next, create a .env file in your project's root directory and add the variable below to it: ASSEMBLYAI_API_KEY = In the next section, you'll get your AssemblyAI API key and add it to this .env file. Get your API key To get your AssemblyAI API key, you need to have an AssemblyAI account; you can sign up for free if you don't have one. If you already have an AssemblyAI account, go ahead and log in . On your welcome dashboard, you should see your API key on the right side of your screen. Click the Copy API key button and paste the API key in your .env file as the value of ASSEMBLYAI_API_KEY . Transcribe Zoom recordings with AssemblyAI Transcribe saved Zoom recordings using the AssemblyAI Node.js SDK. This method works with both local files and cloud URLs. Basic implementation: import client from './assemblyai.js'; const transcribeRecording = async (filePath) => { console.log('Submitting file for transcription:', filePath); const transcript = await client.transcripts.transcribe({ audio: filePath }); if (transcript.status === 'error') { console.error('Transcription failed:', transcript.error); return; } console.log('Transcript:', transcript.text); return transcript; }; transcribeRecording('./path/to/your/zoom_meeting.mp4'); This approach is simple, reliable, and perfect for batch processing multiple recordings. For use cases that require immediate transcription, you'll need to handle live audio, which we'll cover next. Get audio from a Zoom call Live Zoom audio capture requires RTMP streaming to a custom media server. This method enables real-time transcription without saving recordings. Requirements: Zoom Pro plan or higher Custom RTMP server with FFmpeg processing Enabled livestreaming for meetings To stream audio from a Zoom call to a custom media server using RTMP, you must have a Pro plan or higher on Zoom. Additionally, you need to enable livestreaming for meetings on your account. Next, you'll need a custom media server to receive the audio stream from your Zoom call. Create a custom media server To create a custom media server, start by making a new src folder in your project's root directory. Then, create a mediaServer.js file in your src folder with the code below: // mediaServer.js import NodeMediaServer from 'node-media-server'; import processAudioStream from './audioProcessor.js'; const config = { rtmp: { port: 1935, chunk_size: 60000, gop_cache: true, ping: 30, ping_timeout: 60, }, http: { port: 8000, allow_origin: "*", }, }; const nms = new NodeMediaServer(config); // Listen for the "prePublish" event to start processing the audio stream nms.on('prePublish', (id, StreamPath, args) => { console.log(`Stream [${id}] is about to be published at path: ${StreamPath}`); processAudioStream(StreamPath); }); nms.run(); This code sets up a Node.js server for a custom streaming service. It starts by importing the NodeMediaServer library and a processAudioStream function (you'll implement this later). Then, it creates a configuration object for your media server. The config object contains the configuration for your rtmp and http servers. The configuration for RTMP includes the following: port : This option represents the port on which the RTMP server listens for traffic. 1935 is the default port. chunk_size : This option specifies the size of the data chunks that the server sends over the network, and it's measured in bytes. In this configuration, the chunk size is set to 60,000 bytes. gop_cache : Setting gop_cache to true enables the server to cache each stream's latest group of pictures (GOP). ping : This option specifies the interval, in seconds, at which the server sends RTMP ping messages to connected clients to keep the connection alive and measure the round-trip time. In this configuration, the server will send a ping every thirty seconds. ping_timeout : This is the timeout (in seconds) for RTMP ping responses. The server closes the connection if the client doesn't respond to a ping message within this time. In this configuration, the timeout is set to sixty seconds. The configuration for the HTTP server includes the following: port : This is the port number on which the HTTP server will listen for traffic. In this configuration, the port is set to 8000 . allow_origin : This setting specifies which origins can make cross-origin requests to the server. The wildcard * is used in this configuration, meaning the server will accept cross-origin requests from any origin. Explore transcription features in your browser Upload a Zoom recording to see accuracy, speaker labels, and PII redaction—no code required. Open Playground After setting up the configuration object, it creates an instance of NodeMediaServer and listens for the prePublish event. On the prePublish event, it calls the processAudioStream function and passes StreamPath as an argument. You've now set up your custom streaming service. In the next step, you'll use FFmpeg to parse the audio from the RTMP stream. Parse audio from an RTMP stream RTMP streams typically contain both audio and video data multiplexed together. To use the audio data separately, you need to extract it from the combined stream and store it. For this tutorial, you'll store the extracted audio in an MP3 file. To ensure that each audio file has a unique name, you can create a utility function that combines the current date (YYYY-MM-DD) and the timestamp to generate unique file names. Create a utils.js file in your src folder and add the following code to it to implement the logic above: export function getFormattedDateTime() { const now = new Date(); const year = now.getFullYear(); const month = String(now.getMonth() + 1).padStart(2, "0"); const day = String(now.getDate()).padStart(2, "0"); const timestamp = Date.now(); return `${year}${month}${day}_${timestamp}`; } Next, create an audioProcessor.js file in your src folder and add the code block below to implement the logic for parsing the audio and saving the parsed audio to an MP3 file: import ffmpeg from 'fluent-ffmpeg'; import { getFormattedDateTime } from './utils.js'; export default function processAudioStream(streamPath) { const inputPath = `rtmp://localhost:1935${streamPath}`; const outputPath = `./src/recordings/meeting_${getFormattedDateTime()}.mp3`; ffmpeg(inputPath) .outputOptions('-q:a 0') // Set the audio quality to the highest quality .outputOptions('-map a') // Map only the audio streams .on('start', (commandLine) => { console.log('Spawned FFmpeg with command: ' + commandLine); }) .on('progress', (progress) => { console.log('Processing: ' + progress.timemark + '...'); }) .on('error', (err, stdout, stderr) => { console.log('An error occurred: ' + err.message); console.log('FFmpeg stderr: ' + stderr); }) .on('end', () => { console.log('Processing finished!'); }) .save(outputPath); } The code above listens to an RTMP stream, extracts the audio, and saves it as an MP3 file with high quality. It also provides detailed logs for the FFmpeg start , progress , error , and end events. Finally, start your server by running the command below: node src/mediaServer With this setup, once your media server receives an RTMP stream and emits the prePublish event, it will parse the audio from the stream and save it to an MP3 file. Start transcribing Zoom audio with AssemblyAI Now that your server saves MP3 files, create a free account to get an API key and transcribe recordings programmatically. Get API key Make your custom media server accessible with ngrok Currently, your media server is hosted on localhost. You need to make it accessible to Zoom using ngrok. To continue, you need to install ngrok and set it up on your operating system. Then, run the command below to get the location of your ngrok configuration file: ngrok config check cd into the directory returned by the command above, open your ngrok.yml file, and add the configuration below to run your TCP and HTTP ports: tunnels: tcp_tunnel: proto: tcp addr: 1935 http_tunnel: proto: http addr: 8000 You can now run ngrok with the command below: ngrok start --all You should see an output similar to the following in your terminal: Save your forwarding URLs. In the image above, these are tcp://5.tcp.eu.ngrok.io:13156 (this will be your streaming URL) and https://c9f0-105-114-3-2.ngrok-free.app (this will be your livestreaming page URL). Stream audio to your custom live streaming service In an ongoing Zoom call, click the three dots on the bottom right of your screen and select Live on Custom Live Streaming Service : You'll be presented with a form to fill in your livestreaming server's information. The fields in the form include: Streaming URL : The base URL where your stream should be transmitted, which is the forwarding URL for your RTMP server you saved earlier. Change the protocol in the URL from tcp to rtmp . Then, append /live to the end of the URL to specify the route where the stream is directed—for example, rtmp://5.tcp.eu.ngrok.io:13156/live . Streaming key : A unique identifier the streaming server uses to recognize and manage incoming streams. It acts as a password or token that authorizes the stream being sent to the server. You can fill the streaming key with any value of your choice, such as ZOOM . Live streaming page URL : The URL where you can view your stream. In this case, it's your HTTP forwarding URL with the route /admin/streams appended to it—for example, https://c9f0-105-114-3-2.ngrok-free.app/admin/streams . Fill out the fields with their appropriate values and click the Go Live! button: This redirects you to your custom streaming server: https://i.imgur.com/fNjo6ok.jpeg Your custom streaming service is now recording your Zoom call audio and will save it to an MP3 file once your call ends or you end the livestream. Transcribe audio with AssemblyAI Now that you have your Zoom audio, you can get the transcript using AssemblyAI. To achieve this, you need to initialize the AssemblyAI SDK using your API key. Create an assemblyai.js file and add the code block below to initialize your SDK: import 'dotenv/config'; import { AssemblyAI } from 'assemblyai'; // Create a new AssemblyAI client const client = new AssemblyAI({ apiKey: process.env.ASSEMBLYAI_API_KEY, }); export default client; To transcribe a local audio file using AssemblyAI, call the transcribe method on client.transcripts and pass the file path as an argument. Here's a standalone example: import client from './assemblyai.js'; const transcribeAudio = async (filePath) => { const transcript = await client.transcripts.transcribe({ audio: filePath }); if (transcript.status === 'error') { console.error(`Transcription failed: ${transcript.error}`); return; } console.log(transcript.text); return transcript; }; transcribeAudio('src/recordings/FILE_PATH_TO_AUDIO'); In this code, the transcribeAudio function takes a file path as an argument and returns a transcript. If your audio file is stored on the cloud, you can pass the audio URL as an argument to transcribe it. Running the code will return a full transcript of the audio whose location you passed as an argument. Analyze audio with AssemblyAI's LLM Gateway AssemblyAI's LLM Gateway provides a unified interface to apply powerful Large Language Models (LLMs) from providers like Anthropic and Google directly to your audio data. This allows you to perform various tasks on your transcripts, such as asking questions, summarizing content, and generating action items, all through a single, streamlined API. The following example uses a recorded meeting about the "paradox of poverty." You can use the LLM Gateway to summarize it by passing the transcript text and a prompt to the model. import client from './assemblyai.js'; const summarizeAudioWithLLMGateway = async (filePath) => { // First, transcribe the audio file const transcript = await client.transcripts.transcribe({ audio: filePath }); if (transcript.status === 'error') { console.error(`Transcription failed: ${transcript.error}`); return; } // Then, use the transcript text with the LLM Gateway const { choices } = await client.chat.completions.create({ model: 'claude-3-5-sonnet', // Or another suitable model like 'gemini-2.5-pro' messages: [ { role: 'user', content: `Please provide a summary of the following transcript in bullet points. The context is a talk on the paradox of poverty.

Transcript:
${transcript.text}` } ], max_tokens: 500, temperature: 0.3, }); const summary = choices[0].message.content; console.log(summary); return summary; }; summarizeAudioWithLLMGateway('src/recordings/meeting_20240603_1717405934474.mp3'); The code block above will return the summary of the audio file in bullet points. You can also send any prompt of your choice to the LLM to analyze your transcribed audio. You can send prompts to ask specific questions about your audio data, like "How many times was the word 'poverty' used in the meeting?" or "List the examples of welfare traps." For example, the code block below demonstrates how you can use a prompt ("What is the main idea of the talk?") to query your audio data to get the main idea of the audio: import client from './assemblyai.js'; const analyzeAudioWithLLMGateway = async (filePath, prompt) => { // First, transcribe the audio file const transcript = await client.transcripts.transcribe({ audio: filePath }); if (transcript.status === 'error') { console.error(`Transcription failed: ${transcript.error}`); return; } // Then, use the transcript text with the LLM Gateway const { choices } = await client.chat.completions.create({ model: 'claude-3-5-sonnet', messages: [ { role: 'user', content: `${prompt}

Based on this transcript:
${transcript.text}` } ], max_tokens: 500, temperature: 0.3, }); const answer = choices[0].message.content; console.log(answer); return answer; }; analyzeAudioWithLLMGateway( 'src/recordings/meeting_20240603_1717405934474.mp3', 'What is the main idea of the talk?' ); The code block above will return a response detailing the main idea of the audio passed as an argument. Speech Understanding and Guardrails In addition to transcription, AssemblyAI offers a suite of models to extract deeper insights. Speech Understanding models like Sentiment Analysis help interpret the content of the audio. Guardrails , such as PII Redaction and Content Moderation, help ensure your audio data is safe and compliant, addressing what a 2025 market survey identified as a significant challenge for over 30% of tech leaders: data privacy and security. Let's take an example of PII redaction on your audio transcript to minimize sensitive information about individuals by automatically identifying and removing them. To enable PII redaction, you need to add a few configuration parameters. The following code block is a modified version of the transcribeAudio function with the required parameters: import client from './assemblyai.js'; import { PIIRedactionPolicy, PIISubstitutionPolicy } from 'assemblyai'; const transcribeAudioWithPIIRedaction = async (filePath) => { const transcript = await client.transcripts.transcribe({ audio: filePath, redact_pii: true, redact_pii_policies: [ PIIRedactionPolicy.BankingInformation, PIIRedactionPolicy.PhoneNumber, PIIRedactionPolicy.EmailAddress, ], redact_pii_sub: PIISubstitutionPolicy.Hash, }); console.log(transcript.text); return transcript; }; transcribeAudioWithPIIRedaction( 'src/recordings/meeting_20240603_1717405934474.mp3' ); The parameters you added here are as follows: redact_pii : A boolean that enables PII redaction in the transcript when set to true . redact_pii_policies : An array of policies specifying the information to be redacted. The SDK provides an enum, PIIRedactionPolicy , for type-safe policy selection. redact_pii_sub : Specifies the substitution method for redacted information. The SDK provides an enum, PIISubstitutionPolicy , with options like Hash (replaces with ### ) or EntityType (replaces with [entity_type] ). The code block will return a transcript with all the specified PII redacted. You can find the code used in this tutorial in this GitHub repository . Advanced features for meeting analysis Extract structured insights from transcripts using AssemblyAI's audio intelligence models: Speaker diarization To understand who said what, you can enable speaker diarization. This feature identifies and labels each speaker in the conversation. Just add the speaker_labels parameter to your transcription request. const transcript = await client.transcripts.transcribe({ audio: filePath, speaker_labels: true, }); if (transcript.utterances) { // Log each utterance with its speaker for (const utterance of transcript.utterances) { console.log(`Speaker ${utterance.speaker}: ${utterance.text}`); } } Automated meeting summaries Instead of reading a full transcript, you can generate a concise summary using the LLM Gateway. After transcribing the audio, you send the transcript text to the Gateway with a prompt requesting a summary in your desired format, like a paragraph or bullet points. const { choices } = await client.chat.completions.create({ model: 'claude-3-5-sonnet', messages: [{ role: 'user', content: `Summarize the following meeting transcript in bullet points.

Use the LLM Gateway with a specific prompt to extract these key details from the transcript text. const { choices } = await client.chat.completions.create({ model: 'claude-3-5-sonnet', messages: [{ role: 'user', content: `List all action items and decisions from the following meeting transcript.

${transcript.text}` }], max_tokens: 500, }); console.log('Action Items:', choices[0].message.content); Performance optimization and best practices Production implementation best practices: Asynchronous Processing : For long meetings or batch processing, use asynchronous transcription. Submit your file and provide a webhook URL. AssemblyAI will notify your application when the transcript is ready, preventing your server from being tied up waiting for a response. Error Handling : Network issues and other problems can occur. Implement try-catch blocks and check the status of the transcript object. If the status is error , you can log the error message and implement a retry mechanism. Audio Quality : The quality of your transcript depends heavily on the quality of the input audio. When possible, use Zoom's option to record separate audio files for each participant. As noted in multichannel transcription guides , this method allows for Channel Diarization, which can identify speakers with 100% accuracy and significantly improve the overall accuracy of speaker diarization. Next steps In this tutorial, you learned two powerful methods to transcribe and analyze Zoom calls: a simple approach using saved recordings and an advanced method for live streaming. You also saw how to enrich your transcripts with speaker labels, summaries, and action items using AssemblyAI's Voice AI models. With these building blocks, you can create sophisticated applications that unlock the valuable insights trapped in your meeting conversations. To start building, try our API for free . Frequently asked questions about Zoom audio transcription Does Zoom have its own audio transcription? Yes, Zoom provides native transcription for cloud recordings on paid plans. However, developers often use specialized APIs like AssemblyAI for higher accuracy and advanced features. As API documentation shows , this includes capabilities like speaker diarization, PII redaction, and generating action items with models via LLM gateway. Can I get a transcript of a Zoom meeting without recording it? Yes, stream live audio to a custom RTMP server for real-time transcription without saving recordings. This enables live captions and immediate analysis. How do I handle multiple speakers in a Zoom transcript? Enable speaker diarization with speaker_labels: true in your AssemblyAI request. This automatically labels each speaker in the transcript.

title: Siglas corporativas: dicionário prático para o seu negócio
summary: Entenda de forma descomplicada as principais siglas corporativas, em inglês e português, usadas em gestão, finanças, tecnologia e dia a dia.
body_text: Você senta para fechar uma parceria com um fornecedor ou alinhar metas com a equipe e, de repente, a conversa enche de letras. É B2B para cá, KPI para lá, e o ERP que precisa de uma nova integração. Dominar esse vocabulário não é sobre falar difícil, é sobre ter clareza total do que está acontecendo na sua operação. Para facilitar a sua rotina, organizamos as principais siglas corporativas do mercado por áreas . Assim, você vai direto ao ponto nas reuniões e entende os relatórios de ponta a ponta. Cargos executivos Quando você negocia com grandes fornecedores ou busca investidores, é comum esbarrar no chamado C-Level , que é o nível de diretoria de uma empresa. A letra C no início dessas siglas significa Chief (chefe ou líder, em inglês). CEO (Chief Executive Officer) É a presidência executiva, a pessoa que tem a palavra final na empresa. No seu negócio, você exerce o papel de CEO. É a figura que define a visão de futuro, assume os maiores riscos e guia a operação para o crescimento, garantindo que os resultados aconteçam. CFO (Chief Financial Officer) É a diretoria financeira, responsável por cuidar do dinheiro da operação. Quem ocupa essa cadeira analisa o fluxo de caixa , planeja investimentos e garante a lucratividade. Se você faz a gestão do seu próprio caixa, está executando o papel fundamental de um CFO. COO (Chief Operating Officer) É a diretoria de operações, atuando muitas vezes como o braço direito da presidência. O COO foca na rotina pesada: logística, fornecedores e melhoria de processos. A meta principal desse cargo é fazer a operação rodar sem gargalos. CMO (Chief Marketing Officer) É a diretoria de marketing, a mente por trás da comunicação da companhia. Esse profissional desenha a forma como o cliente enxerga a marca. O CMO pensa em campanhas, posicionamento de mercado e estratégias para atrair público e aumentar as vendas. CTO (Chief Technology Officer) É a diretoria de tecnologia e inovação. Responsável pela infraestrutura de sistemas de uma empresa. Se o seu negócio usa um software robusto no caixa ou tem um e-commerce , o trabalho de um CTO é garantir que a tecnologia sustente as vendas sem falhas. Modelos de negócio e expansão Estas siglas definem os formatos comerciais e estratégicos de crescimento da sua empresa. Elas explicam de forma direta para quem você vende e como a sua operação se estrutura para captar recursos, expandir e escalar no mercado. B2B (Business to Business) Traduzido livremente como negócio para negócio. É o modelo em que uma empresa vende produtos ou serviços para outra empresa. Se você compra farinha de um grande moinho para abastecer a sua padaria, essa relação comercial de fornecimento é B2B. B2C (Business to Consumer) Significa negócio para consumidor. É a venda direta para o cliente final, a pessoa física. Quando o morador do bairro entra na sua loja, escolhe os produtos e paga no balcão, a sua operação está atuando no modelo B2C. C2C (Consumer to Consumer) Significa consumidor para consumidor. É o modelo onde pessoas físicas vendem produtos ou serviços para outras pessoas físicas, geralmente usando uma plataforma como intermediária. Por exemplo, quando alguém desapega de roupas em aplicativos de revenda. D2C (Direct to Consumer) A sigla traduzida é direto para o consumidor . Acontece quando a própria fábrica ou a marca que produz o item decide vender direto para o cliente final, cortando atacadistas , distribuidoras e até as lojas do varejo tradicional da jogada. M&A (Mergers and Acquisitions) Significa fusões e aquisições. É o movimento de mercado onde uma empresa compra outra ou duas operações se unem para crescer. Pode parecer coisa de multinacional, mas acontece muito no varejo regional: é quando você decide comprar o ponto comercial do concorrente para expandir sua rede. VC (Venture Capital) O termo significa capital de risco. Trata-se de fundos de investimento que injetam dinheiro em empresas com alto potencial de crescimento. Se o seu negócio tem um modelo inovador e você busca investidores para escalar a operação e abrir novas filiais, o VC é quem assina o cheque. ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) Traduzido como Ambiental, Social e Governança. São as práticas de uma empresa para minimizar impactos na natureza, cuidar bem das pessoas (funcionários e comunidade) e manter uma gestão ética e transparente. Finanças e contabilidade As siglas de finanças e contabilidade representam os relatórios e métricas fundamentais para medir a saúde financeira do seu negócio. Elas indicam se a operação está dando lucro real, como está o retorno sobre os investimentos e para onde o seu caixa está fluindo. DRE (Demonstração do Resultado do Exercício) É um relatório contábil que mostra se a sua empresa deu lucro ou prejuízo em um determinado período. O DRE soma todas as receitas e subtrai os custos e despesas. A linha final desse relatório é o resultado limpo da sua operação. Modelo de DRE: exemplo pronto para você preencher CMV (Custo da Mercadoria Vendida) É o cálculo que soma todos os gastos diretos para produzir, comprar e armazenar o produto que você vende. Se você tem uma loja de roupas, o CMV inclui o valor que você pagou na camiseta ao fornecedor, o frete e os impostos diretos dessa compra. EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization) A sigla assusta, mas significa lucro antes de juros, impostos, depreciação e amortização. No dia a dia, é o seu lucro operacional. Ele mostra quanto o seu negócio gera de dinheiro apenas com a operação principal da loja, antes de impostos ou juros de empréstimos. ROI (Return on Investment) A sigla significa retorno sobre investimento. O ROI mostra quanto volta de lucro para cada real que você coloca na empresa. Se você comprou um forno novo para a padaria, essa métrica revela em quanto tempo o equipamento se paga e começa a gerar lucro real. LTV (Lifetime Value) Traduzido como valor do ciclo de vida do cliente . Ele calcula o quanto um cliente gasta com você ao longo de todo o tempo em que ele continua comprando na sua loja. MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue) Significa receita recorrente mensal. É a previsão de dinheiro que entra no seu caixa todo mês através de vendas de assinaturas ou contratos fixos. Se você fornece marmitas mensais para o escritório vizinho, o MRR é a soma desses pagamentos garantidos. GMV (Gross Merchandise Volume) Significa volume bruto de mercadorias. O GMV é o valor total de tudo que foi vendido na sua loja, física ou virtual, durante um período específico, antes de você descontar as taxas da maquininha, os impostos e os custos operacionais. Indicadores de marketing e crescimento Estas são métricas quantitativas usadas para avaliar a atração, a retenção de clientes e a evolução das vendas do seu negócio. Eles funcionam como um farol estratégico, mostrando onde o seu esforço acerta e o que precisa de ajuste. KPI (Key Performance Indicator) É o indicador-chave de desempenho , a métrica principal que você escolhe acompanhar. Se a sua meta do mês é aumentar a clientela, o número de novos compradores é o seu KPI. Ele é o que mostra se o esforço da sua equipe está trazendo o resultado esperado. OKR (Objectives and Key Results) Traduzido como objetivos e resultados-chave, é um método prático de gestão de metas. O objetivo é para onde você quer ir (exemplo: ser a padaria mais rápida do bairro). Os resultados-chave são as metas menores para provar que você chegou lá (exemplo: reduzir a fila do caixa para menos de 3 minutos). NPS (Net Promoter Score) É a métrica de satisfação que mede a fidelidade do seu público. Você descobre o seu NPS com uma pergunta simples: “De 0 a 10, o quanto você recomendaria nossa loja a um amigo?”. É a forma mais direta de saber se o seu atendimento está conquistando ou afastando seus clientes. CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost) É o custo de aquisição de clientes , ou seja, quanto você gasta para trazer um comprador novo. Se você faz um anúncio pago nas redes sociais, o CAC ajuda a entender se o valor investido compensa o retorno que esse novo cliente deixou no caixa na primeira compra. ROAS (Return on Ad Spend) A sigla significa retorno sobre os gastos com anúncios. Diferente do ROI (que calcula o retorno de um investimento geral), o ROAS mede especificamente o desempenho das suas campanhas de publicidade. Se você patrocinou um post nas redes sociais, essa métrica revela exatamente quantos reais voltaram em vendas para cada real investido. MoM (Month over Month) A tradução é mês contra mês. É a métrica usada para comparar o resultado atual do seu negócio com o mês imediatamente anterior. Se você faturou mais em novembro do que em outubro, você teve um crescimento positivo MoM. YoY (Year over Year) Significa ano contra ano. Aqui você compara o seu resultado atual com o mesmo período do ano anterior. Comparar o faturamento de dezembro com o de novembro engana, mas comparar o seu Natal deste ano com o do ano passado (YoY) mostra o real crescimento. SEO (Search Engine Optimization) Traduzido como otimização para mecanismos de busca. É o conjunto de técnicas usadas para a sua marca aparecer nos primeiros resultados do Google quando alguém pesquisa pelo seu produto. Um bom SEO é o que traz clientes novos de forma orgânica. CTR (Click-Through Rate) Traduzido como taxa de clique. Se você faz anúncios na internet ou dispara e-mails promocionais, o CTR mede a eficiência dessa comunicação. Ele mostra a porcentagem de pessoas que viram a sua propaganda e realmente clicaram nela. Tecnologia e produto As siglas de tecnologia e produto representam os sistemas e infraestruturas digitais que modernizam a operação, conectando as vendas e automatizando as rotinas da sua equipe. ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) É o sistema de gestão empresarial do seu negócio. Sabe quando o caixa, o estoque e as compras não conversam entre si? O ERP é o software que centraliza tudo isso. É ele que tira a sua operação das planilhas e automatiza os processos, do recebimento da mercadoria até a venda. CRM (Customer Relationship Management) É a gestão de relacionamento com o cliente. Na prática, é o sistema que você usa para registrar quem compra com você, quais são as preferências desse cliente e o histórico de compras. Com um CRM, você passa a oferecer o produto certo na hora certa. SaaS (Software as a Service) Significa software como serviço. Esqueça a ideia de comprar um programa pesado e instalar no computador da loja. No modelo SaaS , você acessa um sistema diretamente pela internet, pagando uma mensalidade. API (Application Programming Interface) Em português, interface de programação de aplicações. Pense na API como um “garçom” que leva os pedidos de um sistema para o outro. É graças a ela que o seu sistema de vendas consegue se comunicar automaticamente com o controle de estoque. UX (User Experience) Traduzido como experiência do usuário. A UX é a sensação que o seu cliente tem ao interagir com o seu negócio. Se o seu site carrega rápido, se o catálogo é fácil de navegar no celular ou se o checkout não trava na hora de pagar, você está entregando uma boa experiência. UI (User Interface) Significa interface do usuário e trabalha junto com a UX. Enquanto a UX foca na experiência, a UI cuida do visual. É a disposição dos botões na tela do seu aplicativo de gestão ou a facilidade de encontrar o botão de “comprar” no seu site. NFC (Near Field Communication) A sigla significa comunicação por campo de proximidade. É a tecnologia sem fio que permite a troca de dados em curta distância. Na sua loja, o NFC é o que faz o pagamento por aproximação acontecer. VPN (Virtual Private Network) Significa rede virtual privada. Funciona como um túnel seguro para a internet da sua loja. Se você ou sua equipe precisam acessar dados de vendas remotamente, de casa ou em viagem, a VPN protege essas informações confidenciais contra invasões. Dia a dia corporativo As siglas do dia a dia corporativo são abreviações rápidas muito utilizadas em e-mails, comunicados de logística e ferramentas de mensagens. Elas funcionam como atalhos práticos para informar urgências, prazos ou o status imediato de entregas. ASAP (As Soon As Possible) Significa o quanto antes. Sabe aquele e-mail da transportadora pedindo um documento “ASAP”? É um sinal claro de urgência máxima. O remetente precisa que você resolva a pendência na mesma hora para o processo não travar. FYI (For Your Information) Significa para sua informação. Quando um parceiro encaminha uma mensagem e coloca apenas “FYI”, ele não está cobrando uma ação imediata sua. É apenas um aviso amigável para que você leia e fique ciente do assunto, sem precisar responder. EOD (End of Day) Significa fim do dia. É uma marcação de prazo. Se o seu fornecedor promete enviar a tabela de preços atualizada “até o EOD”, espere receber o arquivo até o encerramento do horário comercial daquele dia. TBD (To Be Determined) A tradução direta é a definir. É muito usado em orçamentos ou cronogramas quando um detalhe ainda não está fechado. Se um parceiro mandar uma proposta com a data de entrega marcada como TBD, significa que ele ainda vai confirmar o prazo exato com você. TBA (To Be Announced) A tradução direta é a ser anunciado. Funciona de forma parecida com o TBD, mas é usado quando uma decisão já foi tomada, porém a informação ainda não pode ser divulgada. Ocorre muito no lançamento de produtos de novos fornecedores. WFH (Work From Home) A sigla significa trabalhar de casa. O WFH é comum naqueles dias em que você precisa focar apenas no fechamento financeiro, longe da movimentação intensa da operação da loja. AFK (Away From Keyboard) Significa longe do teclado. É uma gíria que invadiu as mensagens de trabalho. Quando você precisa sair da frente do computador do escritório para resolver um problema de última hora no estoque, você está AFK. AWOL (Absent Without Official Leave) Traduzido como ausente sem licença oficial. Na rotina do varejo, é aquele funcionário que não apareceu para o turno, não enviou atestado médico e não atende o telefone em um dia de grande movimento. ETA (Estimated Time of Arrival) Significa tempo estimado de chegada. É uma sigla comum na logística. Se você depende de fornecedores semanais, o ETA informa a previsão exata de quando a mercadoria baterá na porta da sua loja. OTP (One Time Password) Significa senha de uso único. É aquele código numérico que chega por SMS para você aprovar uma transação ou login seguro. O OTP é uma camada de proteção essencial contra fraudes no acesso aos sistemas da sua empresa. Gestão de pessoas e cultura As siglas de gestão de pessoas e cultura definem os processos administrativos e as diretrizes voltadas para cuidar da sua equipe e do ambiente de trabalho. Elas cobrem desde o controle da jornada de trabalho até o desenvolvimento da liderança. RH (Recursos Humanos) É a área da empresa responsável pela gestão de pessoas. O RH cuida de tudo que envolve os funcionários, desde a seleção para uma vaga na loja até a folha de pagamento, cálculo de férias, benefícios e o registro de ponto. PDI (Plano de Desenvolvimento Individual) É uma ferramenta muito usada para alinhar o que a empresa espera do funcionário e o que ele precisa aprender. Na prática da loja, é aquele roteiro que você monta para treinar um atendente a virar o gerente do turno. DEI (Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion) A sigla traduzida é Diversidade, Equidade e Inclusão. Montar um time com diferentes vivências e perfis fortalece o ambiente de trabalho. Aplicar o DEI nas suas contratações garante um atendimento mais humano para o público diverso que frequenta seu negócio. PTO (Paid Time Off) A sigla significa tempo de folga remunerado. É o período em que o funcionário está ausente, mas continua recebendo o salário normalmente. Entram nessa conta as férias, folgas e licenças, exigindo muita atenção na hora de montar a escala de atendimento. Rotina e operação Estas siglas corporativas englobam processos do dia a dia, documentações, regulamentações e obrigações que não podem faltar para que sua empresa funcione sem atrito. Elas são a parte burocrática necessária para manter a roda girando na legalidade. CNPJ (Cadastro Nacional da Pessoa Jurídica) É o número de identificação da sua empresa junto à Receita Federal. O CNPJ é o documento básico que formaliza o seu negócio, permite a emissão de notas fiscais, a abertura de contas empresariais e a contratação de funcionários. Sem ele, a sua operação é considerada informal pelo governo. MEI (Microempreendedor Individual) É um modelo simplificado de empresa, criado para formalizar o profissional autônomo. O MEI tem limite de faturamento anual e recolhe impostos através de uma guia única mensal, chamada DAS. É a porta de entrada para quem está começando a empreender . BPO (Business Process Outsourcing) Em português, significa terceirização de processos de negócios. Acontece quando você contrata uma empresa especializada para cuidar de uma área inteira da sua operação. Por exemplo, terceirizar a gestão financeira ou a emissão de notas fiscais para um escritório parceiro. NDA (Non-Disclosure Agreement) Trata-se de um acordo de não divulgação, ou contrato de confidencialidade. Muito comum ao fechar parcerias maiores ou contratar novos fornecedores de tecnologia. Ao assinar um NDA, ambas as partes garantem que as informações estratégicas da empresa não serão vazadas para a concorrência. SKU (Stock Keeping Unit) A sigla traduzida significa unidade de manutenção de estoque. É o código único de identificação que você cria para cada produto do seu armazém. Um tênis branco tamanho 40 precisa ter um SKU diferente do mesmo tênis no tamanho 41. LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados) É a legislação brasileira que cria regras rigorosas sobre como as empresas devem coletar, guardar e usar informações de pessoas físicas. Desrespeitar a LGPD gera multas pesadas para o negócio. Desenvolvimento e gestão ágil Quando a sua loja começa a crescer e a equipe aumenta, manter a organização dos projetos vira um desafio. Entender estes termos ajuda você a liderar o time com mais eficiência, implementando mudanças na operação em menos tempo. MVP (Minimum Viable Product) Significa produto mínimo viável. É a versão mais simples de um projeto que você pode colocar para rodar, gastando o mínimo possível de tempo e dinheiro, para testar se funciona. Em vez de investir meses planejando um serviço de delivery completo, o seu MVP pode ser começar a aceitar pedidos pelo WhatsApp em um bairro específico. SCRUM Não é exatamente uma sigla, mas sim uma metodologia ágil. Trata-se de um modelo de trabalho em equipe focado em entregas rápidas. Nele, grandes projetos são divididos em ciclos curtos. SLA (Service Level Agreement) A sigla representa o acordo de nível de serviço. É o contrato que define a qualidade e o tempo de resposta que um fornecedor promete entregar a você. Se você contrata um sistema de gestão e o SLA garante que qualquer falha será resolvida em até 4 horas, esse é o acordo que você deve cobrar. O conhecimento transforma a gestão Entender as siglas corporativas é essencial para dominar a linguagem dos negócios e tomar decisões com mais autonomia. Quando você sabe o que cada termo significa, as reuniões com fornecedores e o planejamento da equipe passam a ser ações estratégicas para o seu crescimento. Para continuar evoluindo a gestão da sua loja e ter ainda mais clareza sobre os números da operação, conheça a Conta PJ da Stone e descubra como centralizar todas as suas entradas e saídas, fechando o mês sem complicação. Este conteúdo é uma forma de apoiar empreendedores na sua jornada. No entanto, cada estabelecimento é único e nem todas as dicas aqui podem se aplicar ao seu negócio.

title: The Community Behind the Hobby's Biggest Weekend
summary: In 2021, Whatnot showed up to the National Sports Collectors Convention with a 10-foot-by-10-foot booth. One table. Most people walking the floor had never heard of us. body_text: In 2021, Whatnot showed up to the National Sports Collectors Convention with a 10-foot-by-10-foot booth. One table. Most people walking the floor had never heard of us. We've been back every year since, each one bigger than the last. This year we're coming with a 20,000-square-foot space. The distance between that first table and where we are now isn't a story about us. It's about the community that made Whatnot the home of the hobby. Where the hobby lives The hobby found a home on Whatnot fast, and the scale of it now is hard to overstate. Four cards are sold every second, and the number of shows earning more than $100,000 in card sales has climbed over 80% in the past year. Behind those numbers are people: the seller who knows every rookie in the set, the collector who finally tracks down the single they've looked for for years, the buyers who show up week after week for the same show. The hobby has always been about the people in it. Live selling opened new ways to connect, and everything we've built, we've built with the community. The hobby became a career Not long ago, making real money in cards meant a storefront, a spot on the show circuit, and the overhead of both. Live commerce changed that. Someone with deep knowledge of a player, a set, or an era can now build an audience and a business from wherever they are, across singles, vintage, breaks, and everything in between. Three in five sports card sellers on Whatnot made their first sale on the platform this year, and the seller base has grown by nearly half.

title: Teaching our AI agent what's actually in your database
summary: Our chat agent was running 140 introspection queries per benchmark run against customer warehouses just to find the right tables. Here's how we built a schema…
body_text: Most of what our chat agent does is write SQL against a database it has never seen before. A user asks “which customers churned last quarter”, and the agent has to figure out that churn lives in analytics.subscription_events , that the status column is an enum with a canceled value, and that the customers table with 40M rows is the real one while customers_tmp is someone’s forgotten experiment. For a long time our answer to this was: dump the schema into the prompt and hope. That works great on a 12-table Postgres database. It falls apart on a 304-table warehouse, and we watched it fall apart in a specific, measurable way: the agent started running its own information_schema queries against customer warehouses to rediscover what we already knew. In one benchmark run we counted 140 introspection queries against the customer’s warehouse . After the changes in this post, that number is 2. The prompt-side schema, and its compression ladder Every agent turn gets a <database> block: the connected database’s schema rendered as YAML, with tables, columns, types, foreign keys, and enums. The renderer has a character budget (25,000 by default), because schema context competes with conversation history and tool results for the context window. Big schemas don’t fit, so we run an ordered pipeline of compression candidates and take the first one that fits the budget. Each step gives up a little fidelity: Full schema, everything included. Truncate enum value lists, then drop rarely-referenced enums. Drop profiling metadata (more on that below). Deduplicate structurally identical schemas and tables. Fivetran-style warehouses love having staging , dev , and prod schemas with identical shapes, so we render one and note “same structure also applies to: staging, dev”. Truncate tables per schema, keeping foreign-key-important ones. Truncate columns per table, then drop column types, and eventually drop column names entirely. The detail that matters most in that list is what happens to the tables we cut. We don’t silently drop them. The rendered YAML keeps an index line: # other tables (details omitted — use describe_tables): invoices, refunds, tax_rates, ... An agent that has never heard of a table will guess a name or go introspect the live database. An agent that has seen the name but not the details will ask for details, which is exactly the behavior we want. Where the old setup broke down On large warehouses the compression ladder bottoms out hard. A 304-table warehouse compressed to fit 25k characters ends up as mostly table names, and the agent has to fill the gaps somehow. Its only option used to be running SQL against the customer’s warehouse: information_schema.columns queries, SELECT * FROM x LIMIT 5 probes, that kind of thing. This is slow (each one is a network round trip to the customer’s database), and on Snowflake or BigQuery it’s also money, since any query can wake a paused warehouse or bill scanned bytes. It’s a bad feeling to know a customer’s compute woke up because our agent forgot what a column was called. The fix has two halves: give the agent tools to query the schema metadata we already have, and make that metadata rich enough that it rarely needs anything else. Half one: catalog tools We sync schema metadata into our own Postgres whenever a data source connects or refreshes. That means we can answer “what tables mention subscriptions” without touching the customer’s warehouse at all. Two new tools expose that: search_catalog does keyword search over table names, column names, descriptions, and enum values. The ranking took a few iterations to get right. Tokens match at identifier-segment boundaries, so etl matches reverse_etl_sync because it’s a segment of the name, but voice no longer matches invoice . Exact name matches rank above prefix matches, which rank above segment matches, which rank above description mentions. A couple of behaviors we added after watching agents flail: When a search fully resolves to 3 or fewer tables, we inline their complete metadata into the search result. The agent was going to call describe next anyway, so we saved it the round trip. When nothing matches, the result says so, suggests the closest table names by edit distance, and (this one mattered a lot) tells the agent that data values like customer names or environment strings live in rows, not schemas, so it should switch to run_query instead of rephrasing the search 4 more times. Column matches are capped at 5 per table, because warehouse tables all share columns like sync_mode and one table’s boilerplate would otherwise bury every other result. describe_tables returns full metadata for up to 10 tables in one call: every column, type, nullability, foreign keys in both directions, enum values, and the profiling stats below. It also resolves sloppy names. An exact schema.table match wins, then a unique unqualified table name, then a unique near-miss within a small Levenshtein distance. Agents guess table names slightly wrong constantly, and each failed lookup used to cost a full model turn. Now describe_tables("public.usres") just works and tells the agent what it interpreted. The tool descriptions actively push toward batching: describe all your candidate tables in one call, in parallel with other tool calls. Tool-call round trips are the latency budget in an agent loop, so the discovery phase should be as wide and as shallow as possible. Half two: profiling the data, carefully Names and types only get you so far. The queries agents actually get wrong are the ones that need to know what’s in a column: is status a lowercase active or an uppercase ACTIVE ? Is deleted_at null for 95% of rows or 5%? Is this table 300 rows of config or 40M rows of events? So after each schema sync we run a profiling pass that collects, per table: An approximate row count. The newest row timestamp, from the best available updated_at -like column. Per column: sample values for low-cardinality text columns, a null fraction, and a distinct count. The obvious way to do this is COUNT(*) and SELECT DISTINCT over everything, which would be a great way to torch a customer’s warehouse bill. Almost all of the design here is about keeping the probes cheap and bounded: Row counts come from engine catalogs , never COUNT(*) . Postgres statistics, Redshift’s svv_table_info , and so on. (Redshift serializes its numeric row counts as strings like "12400.000000" , which is the kind of thing you only learn by running this against real warehouses.) Engine statistics are read first when they’re free. Postgres’ pg_stats already knows null fractions and distinct counts for analyzed tables. If the engine says a column has 40,000 distinct values, we skip the sample probe entirely, since we’d find more than 8 values and store nothing. Sample probes are SELECT DISTINCT ... LIMIT 9 . If we get 9 rows back, the column is high-cardinality and we store only a “9+” lower bound. If we get 8 or fewer, we know the list is complete, and we store it with that guarantee. Null fractions come from the first 1,000 rows , 30 columns per query, not a full-table scan. It’s an estimate and it’s labeled as one. Warehouses that bill per query get metadata-only profiling. Each dialect’s profiler declares whether data probes are allowed. Snowflake and BigQuery profilers only read catalogs and statistics, so profiling can never wake compute or scan billed bytes. Everything runs inside one global deadline (60 seconds per sync by default) with a 3-worker pool that profiles smallest tables first. Tables over 10M rows skip sampling, tables over 50M rows skip the freshness probe, and a table profiled in the last 24 hours is skipped entirely, so repeated syncs naturally rotate through whatever the last budget didn’t reach. There’s also a hard policy layer: columns marked as obscured in Basedash are never sampled, and neither is any column whose name looks like an identifier, email, URL, token, or hash. Sample values exist to teach the agent the shape of categorical data, and identifiers teach it nothing anyway. One subtle bit we got wrong at first: when the budget expires mid-table, you can’t persist half a column’s results. A column whose distinct-sample probe ran but whose null-fraction probe didn’t would overwrite last week’s good null fraction with an unknown. So a snapshot only includes columns whose probes fully completed, and persistence keeps the previous values for the rest. What the agent actually sees All of this renders back into the same YAML the agent already reads, as comments: subscription_events : # ~2.4M rows, newest 2026-07-20 columns : - id # uuid, PRIMARY KEY - status # text /* all values: active, canceled, past_due, trialing | null fraction: 0 */ - canceled_reason # text /* distinct values: 9+ | null fraction: 0.87 */ - customer_id # uuid, FK → customers.id The all values: label is a promise: the list was exhaustive at profiling time, so the agent can treat it like an enum and write WHERE status = 'canceled' without a scouting query first. distinct values: 9+ is the opposite signal, don’t bother enumerating this. And the row count plus newest-row date answers “is this table real and current” before the agent commits to it. Freshness gets a staleness guard: if the profile itself is more than 7 days old, we drop the newest-row date from the render, because at that point it misleads more than it helps. Row counts drift much slower, so those stay. Measuring it We benchmark the chat agent on an internal eval suite (Chat Bench) that runs scenarios against a 304-table Postgres warehouse, with graded answers and full SQL traces. Two numbers from the catalog rollout: Metric (per full bench run) Before After Introspection queries on the customer’s DB 140 2 Chat Bench score (GPT-5.4) 47.57% 51.53% The score delta is directional (the runs were on different days and the suite has real variance), but the introspection number is the one we were after, and it’s not subtle. Latency and cost stayed flat: the catalog tools added tool calls, but each one is a local Postgres read instead of a warehouse round trip, and the fused search results removed about as many calls as the new tools added. The remaining 2 introspection queries are legitimate, for what it’s worth: dialect-specific edge cases the catalog doesn’t model, which is exactly the fallback role we want live introspection to have. What we took away If your agent is querying a live system to learn things you already know, you’re missing a tool. We had the full schema in our own database the whole time, and the agent simply had no way to ask for it. No amount of prompt tuning fixes that. Never silently drop context, leave a pointer. The single highest-value change in the compression pipeline was keeping omitted table names as an index. An agent can recover from “details omitted, ask for them” but not from “this table doesn’t exist as far as you know”. Design tools around the failure transcripts. The near-miss name resolution, the “data values live in rows” redirect, and the fused describe results all came directly from watching agents waste turns in eval traces. Bound every probe you run against systems you don’t own. Global deadline, per-query limits, catalog-only mode for billed warehouses, and a recency TTL. The profiler’s job is to be invisible on the customer’s side. Label the reliability of derived data. “All values” versus “9+ distinct” versus a rounded null fraction are three different confidence levels, and the agent behaves noticeably better when the rendering makes them distinct. If you like this genre of work, we’ve written up a few adjacent pieces: how a timestamp was busting our prompt cache , paginating user-written SQL across every dialect we support , and what we learned running background jobs on Postgres , which is the queue this profiling job runs on. And if you want to see the agent that reads all this metadata, Basedash is an AI-native BI platform that turns questions into charts and dashboards on top of your own database.

When compliance and payment infrastructure are managed professionally, freelancing no longer feels fragile and becomes a viable long-term career path. ‍ You remain in control of your work, your clients, and your schedule. The difference is that the legal and operational complexity stays in the background, where it belongs, managed by people who understand cross-border requirements better than any individual freelancer. That's not a compromise. That's how independent work should function in a global economy. ‍ But knowing what a CoR does is only part of the picture. Understanding what it *isn't* matters just as much. What a Contractor of Record is Not A Contractor of Record is not your employer. It doesn't assign your tasks, manage your workload, or evaluate your performance. The company you work with still defines the project scope, and you still decide how to deliver it. The CoR exists to manage the legal and payment infrastructure, not to interfere with your professional decisions or creative process. ‍ This distinction matters because the fear many freelancers have when they first hear about a CoR is rooted in a misunderstanding. It sounds formal. Corporate. Like something that might quietly strip away autonomy. That reaction is understandable, but it's based on confusing administrative support with managerial control. You remain responsible for balancing multiple clients, setting your availability, and deciding when and how you work. That's the entire point of being an independent contractor. ‍ The company hiring you will continue to communicate directly with you about deadlines, deliverables, and expectations. The CoR doesn't mediate that relationship or insert itself into project conversations. It processes payments, ensures compliance documentation is correct, and structures contracts properly. Those are back-office functions, not management responsibilities. That's not how it works. You still choose your clients. You still negotiate your rates. You still manage your workload and decide which projects to accept. The CoR doesn't gate your opportunities or restrict who you can work with. ‍ What changes is the administrative layer. Instead of navigating different contract structures, payment methods, and compliance requirements for every client, the CoR standardizes that process. You're not losing control. You're gaining consistency. The difference is that the legal complexity no longer compounds every time you take on a new project in a different country. Missing one of these can lead to unexpected bills or administrative headaches, especially as you take on clients in multiple regions. A CoR stays up to date with local requirements and ensures that taxes are handled correctly, reducing surprises that can drain your time and earnings. ‍ According to Easystaff, remote workers save an average of $4,000 per year on commuting costs. A CoR removes that uncertainty by managing the compliance layer, so you can focus on earning rather than worrying about what you might have missed. title: Dental Marketing in 2026: 7 Strategies That Fill Chairs
summary: Discover 7 data-backed dental marketing strategies for 2026. From local SEO to AI patient engagement, learn what's actually driving growth for dental practices.
body_text: Why Dental Marketing Has Never Been More Critical The U.S. dental industry is booming — and brutally competitive. According to Fortune Business Insights , the U.S. dental services market is projected to reach $165.99 billion in 2026 , with North America generating $189.71 billion across the same period. That's a massive opportunity. But it's one that only well-marketed practices will capture. Here's the uncomfortable reality: there are approximately 200,000 dental practices operating in the U.S. in 2026 , according to Ortho Marketing's 2026 Dental Marketing Stats . That's 200,000 practices competing for the same patients, the same Google rankings, and the same social media attention. And yet, according to SmileVirtual's 2026 State of Dental Practice Marketing Report — cited in Patientdesk.ai's 2026 Dental Marketing Guide — 85% of dental practices still struggle to differentiate themselves , even though they know differentiation is critical for survival. The gap between practices that grow and practices that stagnate isn't clinical skill. It's marketing consistency, channel coverage, and technology adoption. This guide breaks down the seven strategies that are actually moving the needle for dental practices in 2026 — with the data to back every recommendation. 1. Local SEO and Google Maps: Your Most Important Marketing Asset Why Google Maps Placement Determines Your Discoverability If a prospective patient searches "dentist near me" and your practice doesn't appear in the top three Google Maps results, you've effectively lost that patient before they ever knew you existed. According to Dental Marketing Guy's Top Dental Marketing Strategies for 2026 , local SEO and Google Maps visibility are the foundational pillars of dental marketing in 2026 — not a nice-to-have, but the baseline requirement for patient acquisition. Your Google Business Profile (GBP) is the single most important free marketing tool available to your practice. Optimizing it means: Keeping your name, address, and phone number (NAP) consistent across all directories Uploading high-quality photos of your office, team, and treatment rooms regularly Responding to every review — positive and negative — within 48 hours Publishing Google Posts weekly to signal activity to the algorithm Selecting the most accurate primary and secondary business categories Online Reviews Are Now Table Stakes A 2026 survey of 448 dental practices conducted by MouthWatch found that practices treating marketing as essential infrastructure — not an afterthought — consistently report the highest patient satisfaction scores. The report specifically calls out Google presence and online reviews as non-negotiable , not optional extras. "The practices that treat marketing as essential infrastructure — not an afterthought — are the ones reporting 8s and 9s and 10s on the satisfaction scale. The gap between them and everyone else isn't magic. It's consistency." — MouthWatch, 2026 Dental Practice Marketing Survey A steady stream of 4- and 5-star reviews doesn't just build trust with prospective patients — it directly improves your local search ranking. Automate review requests through your patient management system so every completed appointment triggers a follow-up ask. Practices that do this consistently outrank competitors with better clinical reputations but weaker review profiles. On-Page SEO for Dental Websites Beyond your GBP, your website needs to be optimized for local intent. That means: Location-specific service pages (e.g., "Invisalign in Austin, TX" rather than just "Invisalign") Schema markup for dental practices, including hours, services, and accepted insurance Fast mobile load times — Google's Core Web Vitals directly impact ranking Regular blog content targeting long-tail keywords your patients actually search 2. Paid Search: The Fastest Path to New Patient Appointments The ROI Case for Dental PPC Organic SEO takes months to build. Paid search delivers results immediately. According to Ortho Marketing , dental paid search drives 35% of business traffic for dental practices — making it one of the highest-volume patient acquisition channels available. Google Ads for dental practices work best when campaigns are structured around high-intent keywords like: "emergency dentist [city]" "dental implants near me" "teeth whitening [city]" "same-day dental appointment" These searches signal immediate need, which means conversion rates are significantly higher than broad awareness campaigns. Budgeting and Bidding Strategy Successful dental practices in 2026 invest 3–8% of revenue in well-coordinated, multi-channel marketing efforts , according to Patientdesk.ai's 2026 Dental Marketing Guide . For a practice generating $1.5 million annually, that's $45,000–$120,000 per year — a meaningful but justifiable investment when a single implant case can generate $4,000–$6,000 in revenue. Key paid search best practices for 2026: Use Performance Max campaigns alongside traditional search campaigns for broader reach Implement call tracking to attribute phone leads to specific ad campaigns Set up negative keyword lists to exclude irrelevant traffic (e.g., "dental school," "free dental care") Run remarketing campaigns to re-engage website visitors who didn't book Landing Page Optimization Your ad is only as good as the page it sends traffic to. A high-converting dental landing page includes a clear headline, a single call-to-action (book an appointment), social proof (reviews and before/after photos), and a frictionless booking experience. If your landing page requires patients to call during business hours to schedule, you're losing a significant percentage of your paid traffic. 3. Social Media and Video: Where Your Next Patients Are Searching The Social Search Revolution Social media is no longer just a brand awareness channel — it's a search engine. According to Arcane Marketing's 2026 Dental Industry Trends report , 49% of U.S. consumers have used TikTok as a search engine (Adobe Express, February 2026), and 46% of Gen Z prefer social media over traditional search engines (Forbes/Talker Research). This has profound implications for dental marketing. A prospective patient in their 20s looking for a cosmetic dentist isn't necessarily starting their search on Google. They're searching TikTok for "veneers before and after" or Instagram for "teeth whitening results." If your practice has no presence on these platforms, you're invisible to an entire generation of high-value patients. "A dental practice that hasn't posted consistently since 2023 isn't just behind on social. It's invisible in a search environment its potential patients are actively using." — Arcane Marketing, 2026 Dental Industry Trends Video Marketing: The Highest-ROI Content Format Video is the dominant content format in 2026, and the data is unambiguous. According to Wyzowl's 2026 State of Video Marketing Report, cited by Arcane Marketing , 84% of consumers say they want more video content from brands they follow . For dental practices, this is a direct patient acquisition advantage. The most effective video content types for dental practices include: Before-and-after transformation videos (cosmetic cases, Invisalign results) "Day in the life" office tours that reduce new patient anxiety Educational explainers ("What happens during a root canal?") Patient testimonials filmed on-site after treatment Provider introduction videos that build personal connection before the first appointment The cosmetic dentistry market is projected to surpass $5.6 billion by 2026 , growing at approximately 6.4% annually, according to Imagine Your Smile's Dental Health Statistics 2026 . Practices that showcase cosmetic results through video are directly tapping into this high-margin growth segment. Platform Strategy for Dental Practices Not every platform deserves equal investment. Here's how to prioritize: Instagram & TikTok : Visual transformations, short-form educational content, behind-the-scenes Facebook : Community engagement, local targeting for paid ads, older demographics YouTube : Long-form educational content, procedure explainers, SEO-indexed video LinkedIn : Referral network building, DSO partnerships, professional credibility 4. AI-Powered Patient Engagement: From Lead to Booked Appointment The 47% Treatment Acceptance Gap One of the most significant revenue leaks in dental practices isn't a marketing problem — it's a conversion problem. According to Titan Web Agency's 11 Dental Industry Trends Defining 2026 , there is a 47% treatment acceptance gap across dental practices, meaning nearly half of all treatment plans presented go unscheduled. Meanwhile, 55.3% of dentists cite insurance reimbursement pressure as their number one challenge . This is where AI-driven patient engagement becomes a marketing multiplier. Tools like Patientdesk.ai's AI Patient Sales Coordinator are specifically designed to close this gap — automatically following up with patients who received treatment plans but haven't scheduled, using personalized outreach that feels human rather than automated. Recovering even 10–15% of unscheduled treatment plans can add tens of thousands of dollars in annual revenue without spending a single additional dollar on patient acquisition. AI Chatbots and 24/7 Booking According to LinkedIn's Future of Dental Marketing: Trends Shaping 2026 , AI is transitioning from theory to practical application in dental marketing . AI-powered chatbots can now pre-qualify leads, schedule appointments, and handle initial patient inquiries — all without front desk involvement. This matters enormously because patients don't search for dentists only during business hours. A prospective patient who sees your Instagram video at 9 PM on a Tuesday and wants to book an appointment will move on to a competitor if your only option is "call us during office hours." Practices using an AI booking system for dental practices capture these after-hours leads automatically, converting website visitors and social media traffic into confirmed appointments around the clock. Predictive Analytics for Smarter Marketing Spend AI isn't just for patient-facing interactions. Predictive analytics tools are enabling smarter decisions about where to allocate marketing budgets — identifying which channels produce the highest-value patients, which appointment types have the highest no-show risk, and which patient segments are most likely to accept high-value treatment plans. Practices that integrate these tools into their marketing strategy gain a compounding advantage over competitors still relying on gut instinct. 5. The Multi-Touch Patient Journey: 20 Impressions Before Booking Understanding the Modern Patient Decision Cycle One of the most important — and underappreciated — statistics in dental marketing today is this: patients now need to see a dental brand at least 20 times across marketing channels before booking an appointment , according to Patientdesk.ai's 2026 Dental Marketing Guide . Twenty touchpoints. That means a single Google ad or one Instagram post is nowhere near enough. The practices winning in 2026 are those that show up consistently across multiple channels — local SEO, paid search, social media, email, direct mail, and community presence — so that when a patient is finally ready to book, your practice is the one they think of first. Building a Multi-Channel Marketing Ecosystem A coordinated multi-channel strategy looks like this: Awareness : Social media content, video marketing, community sponsorships Consideration : Google search ads, retargeting campaigns, educational blog content Decision : Online reviews, before-and-after galleries, easy online booking Retention : Email newsletters, recall reminders, loyalty programs, referral incentives Each channel reinforces the others. A patient might first discover your practice through a TikTok video, then see your Google ad, then read your reviews, then visit your website — and finally book through your online scheduling tool. Remove any link in that chain and you lose patients who were close to converting. Email Marketing: The Underrated Retention Engine Email remains one of the highest-ROI marketing channels for dental practices, particularly for patient retention and reactivation. A well-segmented email list allows you to: Send recall reminders to patients overdue for hygiene appointments Promote seasonal offers (teeth whitening before summer, back-to-school checkups) Share educational content that positions your practice as a trusted authority Reactivate patients who haven't visited in 18+ months The key is segmentation. Sending the same email to every patient on your list is a missed opportunity. Patients with outstanding treatment plans need different messaging than patients who are fully current on their care. 6. Content Marketing and Thought Leadership Why Content Is a Long-Term Competitive Moat Content marketing — blog posts, videos, podcasts, guides — is the strategy that compounds over time. A well-optimized blog post written today can drive organic traffic for years. A YouTube video explaining dental implants can generate new patient inquiries every month without ongoing ad spend. Patient News' Top 26 Dental Marketing Ideas for 2026 specifically highlights AI search optimization and local authority content as two of the most effective tactics for patient acquisition in 2026. As AI-powered search tools like Google's AI Overviews and ChatGPT become primary research tools for patients, practices that have established content authority are more likely to be cited and recommended by these systems. Topics That Drive Patient Acquisition The most effective dental content addresses the questions patients are already asking: "How much do dental implants cost?" "Is Invisalign worth it?" "What's the difference between a crown and a veneer?" "How do I know if I need a root canal?" "What should I look for in a dentist?" Each of these questions represents a patient in the consideration phase — someone actively researching before they book. A practice that answers these questions thoroughly and authoritatively earns trust before the first phone call. Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) A new discipline emerging in 2026 is Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) — optimizing your content to be cited by AI search tools like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google's AI Overviews. As more patients use these tools to research dental care, practices with well-structured, authoritative content are more likely to appear in AI-generated answers. This is an early-mover advantage that forward-thinking practices are already capitalizing on. 7. Measuring What Matters: Marketing Analytics for Dental Practices The Metrics That Actually Predict Growth Marketing without measurement is guesswork. The practices that consistently outperform their competitors are those that track the right metrics and make data-driven decisions about where to invest. The key performance indicators (KPIs) every dental practice should monitor include: New patient acquisition cost (total marketing spend ÷ new patients acquired) Patient lifetime value (average revenue per patient over their relationship with the practice) Appointment booking rate (percentage of leads that convert to booked appointments) Treatment acceptance rate (percentage of presented treatment plans that are scheduled) Online review volume and rating (tracked monthly, by platform) Website conversion rate (percentage of visitors who take a desired action) Attribution: Knowing Which Channels Drive Results One of the biggest challenges in dental marketing is attribution — understanding which marketing activities are actually driving new patients. Call tracking software assigns unique phone numbers to different marketing channels, so you know whether a patient called after seeing your Google ad, your Facebook post, or your direct mail piece. This data allows you to double down on what's working and cut what isn't. The Consistency Imperative Ultimately, the most important marketing metric is consistency. The MouthWatch survey of 448 dental practices found that practices treating marketing as essential infrastructure — with consistent investment, consistent content production, and consistent measurement — are the ones that report the highest growth and satisfaction scores. Marketing isn't a campaign. It's a system. Building Your 2026 Dental Marketing System The dental practices that will thrive through 2026 and beyond aren't necessarily the ones with the biggest budgets or the most sophisticated technology. They're the ones that show up consistently — in Google search results, in social media feeds, in patient inboxes, and in their communities — and that use smart technology to convert that visibility into booked appointments and accepted treatment plans. The seven strategies outlined in this guide work best when they work together. Local SEO drives organic discovery. Paid search captures high-intent patients immediately. Social media and video build brand familiarity across the 20 touchpoints patients need before booking. AI-powered engagement tools convert leads into appointments and recover revenue from unscheduled treatment plans. Multi-channel presence ensures no patient falls through the cracks. Content marketing builds long-term authority. And rigorous analytics ensure every marketing dollar is working as hard as possible. With the U.S. dental services market projected to reach $165.99 billion in 2026, the opportunity has never been larger. But in a market of 200,000 competing practices, the practices that invest in marketing as infrastructure — not an afterthought — are the ones that will capture it.

body_text: Proposed Acquisition Would Add an Energy-Advantaged, Behind-the-Meter Site Targeted for AI and HPC Compute Development WEST PALM BEACH, FL, July 01, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — AVAX One Technology Ltd. (Nasdaq: AVX) (“AVAX One” or the “Company”) today announced that it has signed a non-binding letter of intent (the “LOI”) to acquire the Bantry Data Site, an energy-advantaged data center site in Alberta, Canada. The proposed acquisition would mark the first step in AVAX One’s power-first data center expansion across Western Canada, building on the Company’s existing Alberta operations and its broader planned AI/HPC infrastructure build-out. The Bantry site fits squarely within AVAX One’s development model, which targets behind-the-meter, energy-advantaged sites capable of supporting modular data center deployments for AI and high-performance computing workloads. “The Bantry Data Site represents exactly the kind of asset we are targeting — an energy-advantaged, behind-the-meter site that can be developed into productive AI and HPC compute capacity on an accelerated timeline,” said Jolie Kahn, CEO of AVAX One. “As we advance our data center initiatives in Western Canada, acquisitions like this enable us to build a robust portfolio of powered sites that support our infrastructure strategy without relying on traditional utility timelines.
